options.why_tempting: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3 on paper. In binary floating point the sum lands a hair above it, so the comparison is false.
Everything equals itself, you would think. NaN is the one value that does not: n == n is false.
Comparing floats with == is allowed, and so is comparing a NaN with itself. Lints may grumble about it, but the compiler accepts both.
In many languages a NaN poisons everything it touches. f64::max is defined to skip a NaN and hand back the other number, so you get the 1.

hint: Three separate floating point facts, one per value printed. Take them one at a time.

explains.what: NaN is not equal to anything, itself included, so n == n is false. f64::max hands back the other number when one side is NaN, so n.max(1.0) is 1, and Display prints the float 1.0 as 1. And 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as a binary value slightly different from the one 0.3 is stored as, so that comparison is false as well.
explains.takeaway: f64 is PartialEq and PartialOrd but not Eq or Ord, because NaN breaks the rules those traits promise. That is why you cannot sort a Vec<f64> with sort(), and why f64::total_cmp exists.
